extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, PTO staff, patent litigators, and policymakers involved in patent law reform
extracted.subtask_description: Legislative and administrative standards and procedural rules enacted or explained in the America Invents Act and its accompanying floor/report text, covering patentability, post-grant procedures, jurisdiction, stays of litigation, grace-period interplay, and business-method review.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO inherent authority to govern procedure and sanction misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office 'has inherent authority to govern procedure before the [Office]' and 'inherent authority to sanction attorneys for misconduct is not restricted to Article III courts' (citing In re Bogese II and In re Bailey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the Office’s existing tools for sanctioning misconduct, there is no need to make the courts into supervisors of attorney conduct in Office proceedings; a practitioner who engaged in substantial misconduct before the Office would likely not escape adequate and effective sanction by the Office itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best-mode requirement not to affect priority entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 15 (conforming subsection (b)) ensures that the best-mode requirement cannot be used to challenge a patent’s entitlement to a right of priority or to the benefit of an earlier filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The effective-date subsection makes this applicable to all 'proceedings' commenced after enactment so it applies immediately in litigation and post-grant reviews under chapter 32.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of deceptive-intent requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 16 (subsections (a)–(h)) reinserts language eliminating various deceptive-intent requirements relating to correcting the naming of the inventor, obtaining a retroactive foreign filing license, seeking section 251 reissue, or enforcing remaining valid claims if a claim is invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminating deceptive-intent requirements moves the U.S. patent system away from subjective intent focus toward a more objective, evidence-based system that will be cheaper to litigate and more efficient to administer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holmes Group fix — preclusion of state-court patent jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 17 enacts the Holmes Group fix (H.R. 2955), abrogating Holmes Group, Inc. v. Vornado and more fully precluding state court jurisdiction over patent legal claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reported bill is modified in two ways: (1) expansion of Federal Circuit jurisdiction is limited to compulsory counterclaims asserting patent rights; and (2) correction so that patent counterclaims that were a basis for removal are not remanded to state court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation to compulsory counterclaims for expanded appellate jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill’s expansion of Federal Circuit jurisdiction is limited to compulsory counterclaims (as defined by Rule 13(a)) asserting patent rights, not to any counterclaim asserting patent rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents defendants from asserting unrelated patent counterclaims solely to manipulate appellate jurisdiction; a permissive counterclaim can be preserved by asserting it in a separate action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand correction for patent and IP counterclaims
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 17(d) corrects an error in prior drafts that would have required remand of patent and other intellectual-property counterclaims after removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The modified text instructs the court not to remand those claims that were a basis for removal (i.e., the intellectual-property counterclaims), avoiding the perverse outcome of remanding the very claims whose removal created jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative review mechanism for business-method patents (Section 18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 creates an administrative mechanism for reviewing the validity of business-method patents, offering a relatively inexpensive administrative alternative to litigation for addressing validity disputes in light of changes such as Bilski.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program is designed to address business-method patents that were issued under earlier, more liberal standards (e.g., State Street) and that may now be invalid under current precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'covered business-method patent' limited to financial products or services
rubrics_metrics.description: At industry request, the definition of 'covered business-method patent' is limited to patents that relate to a financial product or service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many business-method patents are protean, the Office may look to how the patent has been asserted (including patent-owner statements in court or Office proceedings under section 5(g)) to determine whether it reads on products or services particular to financial institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business methods exclude 'technological inventions'
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition’s proviso states that business methods do not include 'technological inventions' — i.e., the definition applies only to abstract business concepts and their implementation, not to inventions relating to computer operations for other uses or to applications of natural sciences or engineering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is intended to preserve review eligibility for abstract business concepts while excluding bona fide technological inventions from the business-method program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office should not rely on non-novel technological recitations to avoid business-method classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18’s definition and authorization are designed so that if a technological element in a patent is not plausibly outside the prior art (e.g., 'off-the-shelf' technology or tech 'known to those skilled in the art'), the Office should not rely on that element to classify the patent as not being a business-method patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents reciting off-the-shelf technology should still be eligible for review under the program; the definition does not require the Office to conduct a merits inquiry into nonobviousness of the technological element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition for review may raise prior-art challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 authorizes raising prior-art challenges in the petition for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows the Office to consider prior art when determining whether a covered business-method patent is invalid, facilitating administrative resolution without litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay-of-litigation standard for Section 18 proceedings (Broadcast Innovation four-factor test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (c) requires a district judge to consider fixed criteria when deciding whether to grant a stay in litigation related to a Section 18 proceeding, incorporating the four-factor test from Broadcast Innovation (and giving separate weight to a fourth factor: whether a stay will reduce the burden of litigation on the parties and the court).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The compromise gives either side a right to interlocutory appeal (review 'may be de novo') and requires the Federal Circuit to ensure consistent application of established precedent. It is expected district judges will liberally grant stays because petitioners must meet a high threshold and proceedings are to be completed within one year to 18 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of consistent application of 'established precedent' in stay decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (2) of subsection (c) requires consistent application of 'established precedent' when courts determine whether to grant a stay, limiting relevant precedent to the body of caselaw applying Broadcast Innovation's four factors in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is intended to ensure predictability and stability in stay decisions across district courts and to limit forum shopping and divergent outcomes based on different trial judges' predilections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace-period interplay between new 102(a) and 102(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative history explains that if an inventor’s actions constitute prior art under new subsection 102(a), those actions necessarily trigger subsection 102(b)’s protections: disclosures by the inventor within the grace period are disregarded as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsection 102(b)(1)(A) is written in broader terms than 102(a)(1), meaning any disclosure by the inventor is disregarded for grace-period protection. If a disclosure is not enabling or not made available to the public, it would not be prior art under 102(a) in the first place; nevertheless, even non-102(a) disclosures fall within the more inclusive protection of 102(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection from others' later disclosures under 102(b)(1)(B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subparagraph 102(b)(1)(B) protects an inventor not only from his/her own disclosure being prior art but also from disclosures of the same subject matter by others that occur after the inventor’s public disclosure, for purposes of 102(a) or 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is designed to give a strong grace period to inventors who have publicly disclosed their inventions prior to filing, benefiting independent and university inventors in particular.

rubrics_metrics.name: New 102(a) public-availability requirement (limiting prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new paragraph 102(a)(1) imposes an overarching requirement for 'availability to the public'—i.e., prior art under 102(a)(1) is limited to subject matter meeting the public accessibility standard (described as 'described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change is intended to remove precedent that treated private offers for sale or secret processes that later result in a public product as patent-defeating prior art; under the new language, those secret/non-public activities will no longer be 102(a) prior art if they were not publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5(g) submission of patent-owner statements to the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5(g) modifies section 301 of title 35 to allow any person to submit to the Office the patent owner’s statements in federal court or in any Office proceeding about the scope of the patent’s claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This submission mechanism helps the Office determine whether a patent reads on products or services characteristic of financial institutions (relevant to deciding whether a patent is a covered business-method patent).
